title: Things That Help: Emails as Letters
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. describes a mental reframe that's made email enjoyable again: imagining each of his three inboxes, work, personal, and blog, as physical mail delivered once a day rather than a constantly-open digital stream. The reframe clarifies that correspondence really only comes in two flavors, urgent, which people use a phone call for anyway, and non-urgent, which can comfortably wait for a scheduled check, undercutting the felt need to monitor email continuously. His operating discipline is OHIO (Only Handle It Once), applied differently across each inbox: work email is processed once daily under a timer, and reader correspondence gets a single protected slot on Friday afternoons that he treats as genuine letter-writing. He backs the mental shift with structural enforcement, having deleted every email app from his phone during COVID and pared personal newsletter subscriptions down to fewer than five. The piece closes by naming the emotional payoff directly: reframing reader correspondence as letters rather than tasks turned his last working hour of the week into one he says he genuinely loves.
points: Stuart reframes his three email inboxes (work, personal, blog) by imagining each as physical mail, which reveals that only two types of correspondence actually exist, urgent (which would use a phone) and non-urgent (which can wait for a single daily or weekly check).
OHIO (Only Handle It Once) is the operating discipline: work email gets processed once daily under a timer, and correspondence from readers gets a single dedicated slot on Friday afternoons.
He removed email entirely from his phone during COVID, a concrete example of the structural, willpower-free boundary he writes about elsewhere as a 'Himalayan boundary.'

Subscription hygiene is treated as a legitimate lever, not a chore: Stuart gave himself blanket permission to unsubscribe from anything he doesn't enjoy seeing, cutting his personal newsletter subscriptions to under five.

The reframe culminates in an explicitly relational payoff; treating reader correspondence as 'letters' rather than tasks turns his Friday email hour into something he says he loves, not merely tolerates.
quotes: What if email didn't exist and all that we had instead was physical mail? Here's how my three sources of email would look in that scenario.
On default, it saturates and addicts. It's always open in a tab. So the second I get an urge to check it, I can.
It's also important to watch that I'm Only Handling It Once (OHIO). OHIO is life-giving — it honors the people who genuinely need to hear back from me (students, parents, colleagues, bosses).
All that we tend to accomplish with undisciplined work email checking is… Anxiety. Tension. Pressure. Like those things? Not me.
About three months into COVID, I realized, "Dude. I'm probably not going to travel any time too soon. Why is email on my phone?" Delete.
A while back I gave myself permission to unsubscribe from literally anything that I didn't like seeing in my inbox. Now I've got less than five email newsletter subscriptions — the rest are toast.

Now… they don't. Because now I know that each Friday afternoon, I get to sit down, C. S. Lewis style, at my writer's desk, and I get to correspond from the fullness of my humanity with other people in the fullness of their humanity.
It's the last working hour of my week, and I love it. So emails are letters.
